text_fidelity_a:
TAG -- Live-Action Elimination Competition -- Eliminate Your Target Until You're The Last One Standing -- 4-10 Players -- Ages 14+ When I was in high school my senior class played an elimination game that was vaguely similar to this (and has been around for years and is still played across the country). Each person drew a name and that was the "target", and there were only loose rules on how to "eliminate" your target (most memorable weapon was a seltzer bottle), and graduation was the time limit. TAG is basically a formalization of that game, with fewer players and more specifics on elimination.

My graduating class had over 500 people, and not all of them played the game. Still, with 50+ players and months to play, it was unwieldy then. TAG limits the game to 10 players max, and the time frame can span anywhere from an hour or two to several weeks. Though the rules are flexible enough to allow for playing for months, this gets a bit cumbersome when having a small player pool.

Each player gets an ID card ("credentials") and a target name. Unlike the more informal version of the game, players are given specific instructions on how to eliminate their target. It might be luring the target to a location or lying in wait, getting the target to do something, or more. Nailing the target with the squirt gun or "poisoning" their food with salt might be fun but if it's not on the specific method card, it doesn't count. Once you've eliminated your target, your next target becomes whoever your original target was stalking. Gameplay continues until there's only one player left.

I like the way this game refines the elimination process, and I like the smaller, more limited scope. This makes it a good game for family events, fun in the dorms at school or even a company morale booster.

If you've ever played the old elimination game, this will be familiar territory. If you haven't it's a fun introduction. There's reasonably good replayability and there's enough flexibility to either play quickly or draw it out for days and weeks.
text_fidelity_b: TAG -- Live-Action Elimination Competition -- Eliminate Your Target Until You're The Last One Standing -- 4-10 Players -- Ages 14+

Dixit Board Game 2021 Refresh | Storytelling Game for Kids and Adults | Fun Family Party Game | Creative Kids Game | Ages 8+ | 3-8 Players | Average Playtime 30 Minutes | Made by Libellud This is a completely different kind of game and the idea of stars and lanterns is abstract. It says it is easy to learn, but to be honest, don't bring your friends together to learn the game. You should set it up, read through the directions and pretend to have two friends with you to understand what is going on. THEN you can explain the game to your friends. The reason is because you can tell this game was not designed in America, there are a few minor English mistakes. The directions have interesting choice of words. So I'm going to try my best by using parentheses to show the words they used in the directions.

The goal of the game is when a word card is revealed, you try to figure out which dixit (picture) cards match that word--by the picture itself, the color(s), inspiration, characters, etc. Then you mark an X (cross) for each dixit card you feel matches that word. At the same time, you want to choose cards you think your friends will choose. If your friends chose that card too, both of you earn stars (sparks) and so on. If they didn't, then you lose (fall) and stop there. If you marked X for too many dixit cards (hoping to get a lot of points), more likely your friends won't have that same card marked and that will make you lose. You have to work like a team, trying to figure out what your friends will choose and win. (This is what they mean by the word, greedy.) This is a good way to teach kids how to perceive the pictures and THINK of others and what they could be thinking, again a "teamwork." This is where it is supposed to be fun. My daughter liked it, but my son didn't like it.

I have one suggestion for you as parents or caregiver of a child age 8 or over. (Ages for the game is for 8+.) I suggest you form the first few turns, you handpick the words you feel your child will be able to "match" then go from there. You handpicking and seeing a few cards in advance honestly does not change the game. The game actually entirely relies on the other players' dixit card choices.

There is one rule that seems pointless. Of course you need to read the directions first to understand what I"m talking about. Here I go anyway--suppose you "fall" then at the end of the game when everyone is ready to score. If you have some sparks and a super-spark from one of your dixit cards that you marked off (crosses), you wipe away one star (but not the super-spark star) then count the remaining stars (sparks). The super-spark star has the same point value as the other sparks so I'm not sure why it makes a difference to wipe off a star or a super-spark star.

This game is Made in China and being sold by a Chinese company on Amazon. It's also created in China and I don't know that it's going to be that great, at least for some U.S. audiences.
text_fidelity_b: Dixit Board Game 2021 Refresh | Storytelling Game for Kids and Adults | Fun Family Party Game | Creative Kids Game | Ages 8+ | 3-8 Players | Average Playtime 30 Minutes | Made by Libellud

text_fidelity_a:
Mattel Barbie Hairtastic Color Stylin Doll As a longtime Barbie collector, I'm always curious when a new Barbie doll uses a gimmick that was popular years ago. In this case, the Barbie Hairtastic Color Styling doll offers the same "color magic" idea that made a 1966 Barbie doll a best-seller. The concept is similar - wet the doll's hair and you can change her hair color using a simple brush and a "foil clip".

This doll comes with a chair, water brush, comb, water bowl (for rinsing the brush), eight "foil" cards (purple, orange and pink), a set of three Barbie hairties, and a styling "foil clip".

The box makes the color transfer seem easy, but actually it takes a bit of work. The instructions say "wet the hair generously" so if you do this with a child, be sure to have a newspaper or towel around so that the doll's hair and the dyes don't stain your table. The foil clip comes already loaded with an orange card, so I tried that first.

The results were mixed. I had to run the clip up and down the hair a few times before the color started to show. I also had to reapply the wet brush several times even though the hair seemed wet enough. Finally, the orange color streak came out bright and strong. Then I tried the purple dye, and the color was faint and weak. I added more water and tried again, but the purple dye failed to transfer a rich color. Not sure why this is.

Contrary to the box claims, the foils can't be reused. It's low-tech - a swatch of watercolor paint on the back of a foil card. When some of the dye from the purple card failed to transfer, I simply took the card out of the clip and rubbed the card itself into the hair. This was sloppy but it did the job better.

The chair has a suction cup, which is a wonderful and long-needed feature. Barbie sat snugly in her chair and it remained firmly anchored while styling. I wish all Barbie chairs had something like this.

Lastly, the instructions don't mention how long the dye will last, only that it comes off with water. Good, but I found that the dye stained my hands and clothing. If a child does this, be prepared. The clip idea is good, but it doesn't fully prevent the process from getting messy.

Overall, it's a decent toy but once the dyes run out, you'd be left with an ordinary Barbie doll.
text_fidelity_b: Mattel Barbie Hairtastic Color Stylin Doll

I really appreciate about actual Legos rather than some of the other brands, that they number the bags and that all of the bricks just fit together so seamlessly and well, to where my kids don't have to constantly bring the bricks and asked me to snap them together. Everything just works. I found the instructions really clear, and while I helped with one or two small places, overall it was easy for my 5 1/2-year-old brick veteran to put together, and a fun build with few to no areas of frustration.

This would make a super gift for an art loving girl. I already have somebody in mind who I might want to purchase the set for for an upcoming birthday.

text_fidelity_a: BARWA 41 Pack Doll Clothes and Accessories 5 PCS Fashion Dresses 5 Tops 5 Pants Outfits 10 PCS Mini Dresses 10shoes 6 Necklace 5 Glasses for 11.5 inch Doll In fact, I just ordered another set. As an adult fashion doll collector and semi-professional photographer, I appreciate the fact that the clothes are from a variety of dolls. Some of the clothes are standard, wide hip Barbie size, while others are slimmer in the hips and torso (more like Model Muse) and still more fit dolls who are short and petite (like Barbie's sisters Skipper and Stacey). The Skipper and Stacey size tops look cute as midriff baring tops on a regular Barbie. I read a complaint below about the pants not fitting, but that's the way Mattel has been making pants since about 1999 when they introduced the first wide hip Barbie doll (the doll that we know today as a regular Barbie). The jeans are meant to fit below the waist and you have to tug to get them on and close them completely because they are meant to fit snugly. It's true, the clothing seams aren't always perfectly straight, but I have the same issue with Mattel Barbie clothes that I buy in person. Plus, the fabrics for these fashions are - for the most part - nicer than what Mattel has been offering lately. At the end of the day, when you consider that SINGLE ITEM Barbie brand clothing packs currently sell for $2.44 - $5.00 each, and Barbie brand complete fashion sets with shoes retail for $5.00 - $35.00 each, spending just under $2.00 for complete outfit is a great deal.

Mainstreet Classics Dutchman 3-in-1 Combo Folding Board Game Set This MAINSTREET CLASSICS DUTCHMAN 3-IN-1 COMBO FOLDING BOARD GAME SET delivers pretty good value for the money (about $37 on Amazon). Maybe it’s a bit expensive for what it is, but it’s all made of wood. On the outside of the case is an inlaid wooden chess/checkers board; on the inside, a somewhat compressed inlaid wooden backgammon board. The case folds closed (with a handle) so that it can hold wooden checkers, wooden chess pieces, wooden dice cups, and backgammon dice.

My game set has none of the quality control issues complained of by other reviewers (no blobs of glue, loose hinges, etc.). The chess pieces won’t win any design awards, but they are playable because they are easily recognizable as pawn, knight, rook, etc. The checkers are small, but are reasonably sized for a portable game set. The case is sanded smooth and has a lacquer finish.

I think this is a great game set to carry along on vacation, or to leave year-round at a cabin or second home. It is a decent starter set for kids, especially for kids interested in learning chess.

Star Wars Boba Fett Plush 8-Inch Character Figure From the Book of Boba Fett, Soft Doll Dressed in Classic Look I have a whole Star Wars bookshelf for my EU books and Legos. This plush Boba Fett from Mattel fits right on that shelf.

The details are nice. Some of his accessories are made from faux leather or felt or plastic. Those details look cool and add to the look of the plush.

Boba Fett doesn’t sit or stand up on his own, but he will stay sitting up if leaned against something. The huge head makes it impossible for him to balance on his own.

Construction is okay. The plush should hold up to lots of playing from kids. Boba Fett does have something plastic at the base of his head, it feels like a big disc to give shape to the bottom of his helmet. But otherwise, he is soft. I did feel and see a lot of thread knots, like on his hands and on his helmet rangefinder. But that is me nitpicking.

I wish Mattel had done a better job with the packaging. The plush comes inside a plastic bag -- that’s it. My plastic bag had a hole in it and his cape fell out, so I nearly cut it when I was opening the envelope he shipped in. The tag got all bent up and creased, which I wasn’t happy about. I keep the tags on almost all of my Star Wars merch, so having this one be bent up in transit wasn’t ideal. This probably isn’t a big deal for kids, but some adults might not be happy.

Magical Fairy Adventure – Fun Activities, Surprises, and Clues Magically Appear in an Enchanted Fairy House For this kit, you're paying for the convenience of having everything organized and already there. Also, for the "magical" experience you can provide for your child. If you do "Elf on a Shelf" or Santa Clause or anything similar, you'll probably love the added magical part of this kit. (We don't. We're all different and that's okay.) The parent has to be very involved. It's not a kit you just hand over to the child. (The parent portion is in a well sealed container to help keep the secret, since I imagine many parents will attempt to hand it straight over to the child. That was my plan before I realized what it was.) The child will have to do activities, and then the parent will secretly leave another activity in the fairy house. This is suppose to make the child believe the fairies left them a gift. (For example: The child is to craft 3 fairy bells and hang them around their room. Inside the fairy house, they'll place a stick, pebbles, and a leaf. They'll then spin the house and ring each bell to summon a fairy visit.)

The quality is similar to the various "Box of the Month" type subscriptions out there for kids. In my opinion, there's more in the wizard kit. There is the same amount of activities in both, but there's just not as much to do in this fairy kit. (It seems more stickers and easy crafts.) It's not high quality, but it's still nice enough. The crafts are something that could be put together with supplies from a dollar store. But, it's so convenient having everything in one place, especially for a disorganized person, like myself. Plus, there'd the "magical" experience provided for those that desire it.

Though the wizard kit that is similar to this one could work for boys and girls(and this one still could, if desired), this fairy kit is definitely targeted to girls. At the end, I couldn't help but feel sorry for all the little children doing these activities, hoping to see a fairy. While gifts are left, which are supposed to let the child know a fairy visited them, they'll never actually see one, unless the parent does something extra. We just did the crafts, since we don't do imaginary things as real. Without the added magical element, though, this kit just doesn't hold near as much value. If you're like us and don't do Santa and all, I'd recommend another kind of kit. If you do love the idea of pretending fairies are leaving gifts, this might be a blast for you and your child, as long as you don't think they'll be too disappointed that they never actually see a fairy. Overall, I found it a little disappointing, particularly considering the current price(which changes constantly).
text_fidelity_b: Magical Fairy Adventure – Fun Activities, Surprises, and Clues Magically Appear in an Enchanted Fairy House

LiangCuber Tornado V3 M Flagship Speed Cube QY Toys X Man Tornado V3 Magnetic 3x3 Cube (Tornado V3 M Magnetic Core Flagship) When I got this, I still didn't solve the Rubik's cube. I know there are all kinds of tutorials, but I wanted to solve it on my own. Fast-forward 11 years later, I flipped the table (so to speak) and watched a couple tutorials. This was the cube I used to solve the puzzle for the first time. I watched a couple videos of the cube before receiving mine to get a better understanding of the mechanisms and design. During my first session, I set the magnets to the strongest and left the dials as they were. Two hours is how long it took me to solve it on the first try.

I like that this cube comes with a handful of accessories. I use the case to carry the cube with me to and from work. It stays on my desk; whenever I have to read something on my monitors and not use the keyboard, I solve a little bit. Now I can solve the cube in minutes, though it took me a few days to get to this point. I now have the spring and tension set to the strongest for how much force can be pulled and weakest for how fast turns can be. (Apologies for not using the correct terms, but I tried looking up what the dials exactly do and I still can't figure out which does what with regard to the terminology, but I base it off feel.)

The cube comes with a leather bag and a tool to adjust the magnets. The first time I accessed the dials, I used a pen to pop off the tiles. They can be difficult to pull off by hand alone, even after being pulled so many times. The lever for each dial also was difficult to pull. Now, I leave it semi-flush to the dial to make it easier to access in the future. They also pop off easily, but are [somewhat] easy to put back. The magnet levels sometimes move on their own. If I happen to notice a magnet at a strength I didn't set it at, I'll re-adjust. Annoying, but an easy fix. I no longer use the tool that came with the cube because any item small and flat enough will work. The bag is kept in the box for now.

There are two manuals that come with the cube: one for the cube itself and the other on how to solve it. I tried using the solve tutorial but found it confusing with some typographical errors, so I used videos. I learn better visually anyway. Even though the cube's manual has great illustrations for the mechanics, I failed to understand what they actually do, so I looked up videos for that too.

This is the third cube I own and currently it's my favorite. Each time my time lowers after solving, I adjust the settings. I'm becoming a speedcuber without realizing it.

Thames & Kosmos Pepper Mint in The Fantastic Underwater Science Voyage Experiment Kit I’m a big fan of the Thames & Kosmos building kits--especially the ones that teach STEM principles. However, this THAMES & KOSMOS PEPPER MINT IN THE FANTASTIC UNDERWATER SCIENCE VOYAGE EXPERIMENT KIT is definitely NOT one of my favorites. The experiments do teach about the physical properties of water (e.g., siphoning, hydraulics), but they are boring--mostly they require operating a syringe to push water through tubing.

The boat is easy to build. The parts are stamped onto thin sheets of wood. You punch the parts out of the sheets, and the edges come out smooth and clean. The parts then lock together without requiring glue or other fasteners. The assembly instructions are included in a booklet that contains a silly adventure/discovery story that features the girl character Pepper Mint.

The story is interrupted from time to time with instructions for science experiments. Each experiment has a good, easy-to-understand explanation of “what’s happening” (e.g., water can move things because, unlike air, it cannot be compressed).

The kit is apparently aimed at 11-year-old girls (Pepper Mint’s age), but the story and the experiments seem rather simplistic for that age group. I do wish that Thames & Kosmos had chosen a more serious name than “Pepper Mint” for their girl scientist. This kit has some teaching value, but it trivializes science for girls.
text_fidelity_b: Thames & Kosmos Pepper Mint in The Fantastic Underwater Science Voyage Experiment Kit

It takes what I love from Liar's Dice, but gives it more suspense in my opinion. It wouldn't be difficult not even slightly, with no rules adaptations other than changing the skulls to faces, and flowers to numbers. That shouldn't dissuade you from purchasing this though, this is a really cool set, that will last a good amount of time, and it is a nice bit of decoration anyway with that pretty box! text_fidelity_a: Power Wheels Kawasaki Lil' Quad The power wheels kawasaki lil' quad is a great toy for a toddler. You will want to make sure that your little one has enough flat space to drive around because the turning radius is extremely wide. You will need a very large space to make a complete circle. Also, there is no reverse button. You should not ride this near hills, slopes, pools, roads, cars, or anywhere else that could increase the chances of an accident. You should also note that even if the "go" button is not being pressed the quad can reach high speeds if on a steep incline.  It comes with a rechargeable 6v 4Ah battery and charging cord that is to be plugged into a wall outlet (not a ceiling outlet!). Before using for the first time the battery must be charged for 18 hours, and 14 hours after each use. You are warned not to leave the battery charging for longer than 30 hours or it may cause the battery to degrade. The biggest downside is that there is no light to denote the battery is charging or completely charged. You just have to assume it is charging and that the battery is completely charged after you unplug it. It requires about 10 minutes of assembly time (excluding the sticker time). The quad does not come with the stickers already placed, so you will need to place the stickers on yourself. You will need a philips head and a flat head screw driver, all other parts are included. I was afraid to force it to completely connect and potentially breaking the plastic connector. It is listed to be for 12-36 months, and up to 40 pounds. Personally, I think 12 months is a little young to be riding this, especially if your child is on the small side and not completely steady on their feet when walking. Made in China.

text_fidelity_a:
The Lord of the Rings: The Card Game Revised Core Set | Adventure/Cooperative Game for Adults and Teens | Ages 14+ | 1-4 Players | Average Playtime 30-120 Minutes | Made by Fantasy Flight Games The first TCG I was hooked on was Pokémon, which was about 10 years ago. I grew up with the Pokécraze in the 90s, and still collect the cards. Thankfully, I full unlimited sets of the first three sets. Over time, and of course with life's changes and demands, I stopped playing the game. Thank goodness, too, because what a money sink that can be. I played MtG for a bit, but thankfully convinced myself to stop playing because of the money factor alone. But I still love playing card games because of the physical cards and the resource management. Then I discovered Fantasy Flight's LCGs. I got into tabletop games from Europe before TCGs, so I was familiar with Fantasy Flight. I found out about their Lord of the Rings Card Game when it was first announced, but didn't bother to understand what an LCG was. With the pandemic, my interest in tabletop games peaked, but I still didn't want to get into TCGs. Then I was reminded of this game with the re-release and ordered the Core Set. What a wise choice.

The rules are a beast to master, but they are clear and guide you with a comforting hand without feeling like they're holding your hand like it's a child's. If ever I was confused, all I had to do was look in another section of the manual and my confusion dissipated. To start, the game comes in that oh-so-ever-nice cardboard box Fantasy Flight games are known for. Upon opening, the game greets you with the rule book, an instruction guide, sheets of tokens and build-your-own life counters (Who doesn't live opening those fresh token sheets and popping them out?!) and a plastic insert with the sealed cards. What did I do next? Go to Board Game Geek and look up sweet printables the community made. Using the insert alone, I was able to organize the cards in a utilitarian manner. While the tokens and life counters provided are nice, I used third-party options that I'll explain later below.

Finally, I sat down one night, blocked off two hours, and opened the instruction manual. The manual gives four starter decks to build. I built each played each against the first scenario. The first game took me the full two hours due to the learning curve. There's definitely a lot to keep track of. The game uses some mechanics from other TCGs, but does so in a way that makes it feel like I'm actually in a Middle-earth adventure. Almost like a choose-your-own adventure. Because the game can be played solo, I took my time to absorb every step and read each card's text in full. I know there can be only so much text on the small cards, but the font is *teeny*. The game certainly needs a well-lit table.

After I tested each deck, I moved on to the next scenario, which helped me nearly memorize all the steps. To this day, I sometimes forget a step, so I made my own mini rule book that fits inside a deck box. (By the way, I use an Ultimate Guard Twin Flip'n'Tray, which comfortably holds two decks and the scenario deck--all double-sleeved--a handful of dividers, and two slim life counters.) Once I got to the third scenario, though, I hit a block. Another reason I steered clear from TCGs is the process of deck-building. It's long, tedious, and I just don't want to use what little time and memory I have to maintain decks. Thankfully, the years before the re-release have seen lots of contributions from the community. I recommend going to the game's Subreddit, which provides extremely useful and informative links on deck-building and steps for beginners. With Beorn's Path, I finally found fantastic decks to crush the third scenario--mostly. It's still a monster. Before the third scenario, I was hesitant on using more than one deck while playing solo. Keeping track of all those steps twice intimidated me, but I realized playing the third scenario with just one is impossible and only will cause you torment. Plus, there are mechanics that are available only with more than one deck. Once I confronted my fear, I soon realized how much more fun I was missing out on from using only one deck. The game does a wonderful job at incorporating other players.

The game is fun, but can be frustrating. Some enemies are obscenely strong, and the rules (if followed strictly, which I do) can be unforgiving to follow. Playing a scenario for two hours or more only to lose makes for a frustrating experience. I thought finally beating the third scenario would be cathartic, but it was underwhelming. I won! ...Yay... The only prize was putting all those parts away.

Now for the accessories. If a game has a good following on Board Game Geek, chances are the community will make fun accessories or suggestions of accessories to use. LotR: LCG utilizes turning the cards and tokens to show certain choices made throughout the game. This became a tedious process and quite messy; moving all those parts every step became a burden. Plus, the game needs a *lot* of table space. After consulting the internet and performing my own trials and errors, I've come to the setup in the picture attached to this review.

- d20 for first-player token and round count
- Thin, plastic life counters that I can store in the deck box
- White and black stones for unperformed actions
- Small d6 for anything requiring numbers (life, quest progress, resource, etc.)
- d10 for heads/tails and randomizer
- Wooden card stand for staging area (optional, but helps)
- Large mouse pad for gaming area; I didn't like the large options game companies offer, and found that a large mouse pad met the size I needed and is very inexpensive compared to “official” options
- Deck box trays to hold player cards and unused tokens
- Beverage and edible optional, but strongly recommended

This may seem to cause confusion, but this is what helps me keep track of every possible option in the game without getting lost or having to move a lot of cards/pieces compared to what's in the box. Yes, it adds more cost to the game, but it's completely optional. While this provides what I require for the Core Set, I will amend or append as necessary with each expansion.

I finally found a card game I can play on my own and enjoy without having to pay big bucks.

Note: If any of the review is confusing, please let me know. I never edit my reviews, but am more than happy to help.
text_fidelity_b: The Lord of the Rings: The Card Game Revised Core Set | Adventure/Cooperative Game for Adults and Teens | Ages 14+ | 1-4 Players | Average Playtime 30-120 Minutes | Made by Fantasy Flight Games

text_fidelity_a:
Harry Potter Lexicon-GO! Word Game Lexicon Go is a very fast-paced, easy-to-play word game using a deck of 52 plastic tiles, each with a letter of the alphabet. the tiles are arranged face down on the playing area, and each player draws 10 tiles from the deck. The goal is to arrange all 10 of your tiles into words as quickly as possible. If you're unable to use all of your letters to make words, you can swap out a tile (within certain parameters) or you can play on other players' words. The first player to use all 10 tiles wins the round. Win five rounds and you've won the game.

We played this game with two, three, four, and five adult players. I would guess that in at least 8 out of 10 rounds, one player was able to use all of her letters to form words without any swapping out or playing on another player's tiles -- which made the game move very, very quickly, , but also made it a little bit boring. There is very little strategizing and interaction. The best part was challenging words and learning the meaning of funny new words.

This was a little bit too fast-paced and frenetic for my tastes, and whether you could use all your tiles on the first draw depended primarily on getting a good vowel to consonant ratio- if you draw at least three vowels, it's pretty easy to make two, three, or four letter words to use all ten tiles. If you draw only one or two vowels, you will have a tough time using all your tiles.

The game is fun, clever, and well-made. The carrying case is well-made and the tiles are nice quality. This would be a great family game or vacation game, and it worked equally well with two players as it did with five players -- it just worked differently. It is versatile. If you're a fan of Scrabble or the New York Times crossword, this seems very fast-paced and a little too easy. It may better suited for younger players -- maybe elementary school-aged children.
text_fidelity_b: Harry Potter Lexicon-GO! Word Game

text_fidelity_a:
Pink Racer This is a fun and powerful little racing ATV that my kids, ages nearly 5 and seven, have a lot of fun playing with. We have another power wheels vehicle that we call "purple thing" because it has three larger wheels and is set a lot closer to the ground. That one, grips onto our lawn and has a lot of power for going up and down the small hills in our grassy yard.

This one, seems to even have more power than our last one, but unfortunately the tires are less grippy, so it ends up spinning out and people get stuck trying to go up a hill and have to strategize about what long and circuitous route they can take to get up the hill kind of sideways so that it doesn't lose power or more usually, spin its wheels.

This thing goes a bit faster than our other one, and has a feel of power to it, so I really think the wheels and their slippery, hard surface, are the issue. This is gotten slightly better with use over the last few months, but unfortunately is still happening very frequently when in use. We have found the issue is just as bad on our concrete driveway as it is on our grass. Our grass is a bumpy, country lawn that is generally on watered in summer and goes kind of brown and dry.

I also think they could've improved it by potentially making it big enough to seat a second, smaller child. Our other one is big enough that when our son was five and our daughter was three, she could sit behind him as he drove around the yard.

Overall, if you have a very flat, large lawn that a child would be unlikely to spin out the tires on, this is a really fun, immediately thrilling toy to play with, has a ton of power, multiple settings that are fun for the kids to experiment with, and is very maneuverable and controllable. However, for bumpier lawns or yards with some minor grade changes and hills, this might not be the best choice for getting around.
text_fidelity_b: Pink Racer

My First Sewing Kit by Alex Crafts, Perfect for Beginners, Arts and Crafts Colorful and Fun Sewing Projects to Learn the Basic Skills of Sewing (Ages 7+) This possibly isn't the best starter kit for a child who has never sewn before. The instructions aren't that good. If the child has done any other sewing, or has anyone who can help (can be another kid) then this will provide a great deal of practice, which is where this really shines.

There are quite a few projects here. There is a draw string bag, a stuffed cat, a stuffed dog, a stuffed elephant, and a book cover with pencil holder wrapper.

For supplies, it has everything - scissor, tape measure, pins, pin cushion, button, even some extra stuff, like pop poms, that you won't need for any of the projects. There definitely is not even close to enough stuffing. It did not quite fill the cat, which is the first, and smallest, of the stuffed animal projects. You'll want to pick up something like [[ASIN:B000YZ7G44 Fairfield Poly-Fil Premium Polyester Fiber, White, 1 Bag, 12-Ounce]]. Any fiberfill will do, but this is a good one, similar to what is in the kit. While on the topic of stuffing, a double pointed knitting needle, or better http://www.amazon.com/Little-Foot-That-Purple-Thang-/dp/B001ELBCFG/ref=sr_1_1?ie=UTF8&qid=1464647654&sr=8-1&keywords=purple+thang will help get the stuffing into the tight areas, like the tails. Both the fiberfill and the thang will be useful items in a variety of sewing projects.

For the embroidery floss, it says to cut the skein on one side to make lengths. That works, no issue, but it might be better to make a little yarn butterfly (really simple; instructions are online) so that you can pull the length you need for each section and the leftovers, and there will be plenty, can be used to make friendship bracelets. There is an excess of embroidery floss here.
text_fidelity_b: My First Sewing Kit by Alex Crafts, Perfect for Beginners, Arts and Crafts Colorful and Fun Sewing Projects to Learn the Basic Skills of Sewing (Ages 7+)

I do like this toy but I do think it has a bit of a niche audience. If you're cool with keeping it away from the youngins and playing with it in an open area where noise isn't an issue,- it's probably more of a 4.

Wonder Wheels by Battat – Dump Truck, Tow Truck, Cement Truck – Toy Truck Combo Set for Toddlers Age 1 & Up (3 Pc) – 100% Recyclable , Yellow This is a mixed bag. The dump truck is GREAT! Much better than the green toys version because the dump part goes all the way vertical to dump out. YAY!!! My 5 year old was all over this, mixing all manner of unappetizing mud pies, twig sandwiches and grass clumps and moving the muck from one place to another.

The cement mixer is AWFUL. It is infuriating that they make a cement mixer with no opening to put stuff! It has this tiny little grate that lets out small amounts of dry sand or very teeny tiny pebbles. I guess you are supposed to cram it in through the tiny grate that is supposed to let stuff out? God forbid you get dirt in there and water, and it clumps up, as has happened with many other trucks in a similar vein. I had no issue turning the drum smoothly and appreciate that the drum can be angled downward to dump out, but this was pretty much the most disappointing disaster of a cement mixer I could imagine given there is no mechanism for getting stuff IN, or cleaning it. Who DOES that? That designer or committee needs to be fired.

The tow truck is mixed. I love the pull out ramp. It sticks a bit and is a little harder to use than desired, but overall good. But the hook part and the bar do not function well. The hook is stuck onto this boxy bar so it is hard to actually get it to hook to a vehicle, not impossible, but could have been done better. You can pull the bar out an inch and a half but then trying to push it back in, I injured myself/ hurt my finger. I am a grownup, so it is hard to imagine that this was truly vetted for use by toddlers if it needs that much force. Then the angling mechanism also requires a lot of oomph. My five year old can do it but finds it frustrating. 2 year old cannot.

Overall the packaging of having this set of three harmonizing full size trucks is great. Would be fun to pull out when guests come to loosen everyone up together and give everyone something to play with. But the design flaws make it hard to truly recommend. In a dry, clean sandbox, this would probably be most successful since the cement mixer would actually function.
text_fidelity_b: Wonder Wheels by Battat – Dump Truck, Tow Truck, Cement Truck – Toy Truck Combo Set for Toddlers Age 1 & Up (3 Pc) – 100% Recyclable , Yellow

LEGO Disney Frozen Elsa's Magical Ice Palace 43172 Toy Castle Building Kit with Mini Dolls, Castle Playset with Popular Frozen Characters Including Elsa, Olaf, Anna and More (701 Pieces) This LEGO DISNEY PRINCESS ELSA’S MAGICAL ICE PALACE 43172 TOY CASTLE BUILDING SET (New 2019; 701 Pieces) is a reissue of the previously discontinued 41148 set of the same name that was originally released in 2017 (also at a retail price of $79.99). Some of the ad pages in the 43172 building instructions are different, but the models are the same.

The Elsa’s Magical Castle model isn’t large, but it has loads of sparkle and detail; and tons of play potential in the many accessories (e,g., castle furniture, Olaf’s train) and moving parts (e,g., swirling staircase, snow slide). It’s one of my all-time favorite LEGO buildings--one that I have on permanent display (alongside my big Disney castle model).

What I love most about Elsa’s castle is that it incorporates a lot of transparent “Frozen blue” bricks, many of which have embedded silver sparkles. I love shiny stuff, and Elsa’s shimmering cape is something to behold. I also love trains, so Olaf’s train is another plus. The little snowmen’s teeter-totter (near the snow fort) is fun. I don’t really care for the scary snow monster, but it helps in reenacting scenes from the movie.

Some of the model’s sparkle is added with stickers, but there aren’t a lot of stickers, and they’re easy to apply. There is a moving slide that opens and closes the tall castle front doors. There is a spiral staircase that swirls open when you turn a knob. The figures of Elsa and Anna are true to the cartoon figures in the Frozen film. This is truly a great, classic LEGO set, based on a great, classic Disney movie.
